concepts: Cobalt Strike: commercial C2 framework with Team Server, Beacon (implant), Malleable C2 profiles, and Aggressor Scripts
Sliver: open-source C2 framework with implants (Go-based), supports mutual TLS, WireGuard, and HTTP(S)
Mythic: modular C2 framework with pluggable agents and C2 profiles — separates UI, API, and agents
Havoc: open-source C2 with modern UI, supports sleep mask and indirect syscalls
C2 communication methods: HTTP(S) beacons, DNS tunneling, SMB named pipes, TCP listeners
Malleable C2 profiles: customize beacon traffic to blend with legitimate web traffic
key_facts: Cobalt Strike Beacon is the most widely used (and detected) C2 implant — Malleable C2 profiles customize its network signatures
Sliver implants are compiled Go binaries — larger file size but harder to detect than Cobalt Strike
DNS C2 tunneling: beaconing via DNS queries to attacker-controlled domain — bypasses egress firewall rules
SMB named pipe C2: beacons communicate through SMB named pipes for air-gapped pivot communication
Cobalt Strike sleep mask: encrypts beacon memory during sleep period to evade memory scanning

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: C2 communication creates periodic network connections (beaconing) to external IPs/domains. Blue team sees: regular interval connections (jitter patterns), DNS tunneling patterns, TLS certificate anomalies, known C2 IP/domain reputation hits, and beaconing behavioral patterns.
logs: DNS logs (DNS tunneling patterns, high-volume queries to single domain)
Sysmon Event 3 (network connections from suspicious processes)
detections: DNS tunneling detection (high entropy, long subdomains)
Threat intel: known C2 IP/domain reputation matching
JA3/JA3S TLS fingerprinting for C2 clients
Sigma: known C2 framework signatures (Cobalt Strike default certificates)

drills: Set up a Sliver or Havoc C2 server in a lab and generate an implant that beacons over HTTPS
Create a Malleable C2 profile for Cobalt Strike that mimics legitimate Amazon AWS traffic
Configure a DNS C2 channel and detect it using Zeek DNS analysis in the lab SIEM
common_mistakes: Using default Cobalt Strike certificates and ports (50050 for Team Server) — immediately detected
Beaconing with no jitter (perfect intervals) — behavioral detection tools flag regular periodic connections
Not using domain fronting or redirectors to hide the real C2 server IP

topics.title: Covert C2 Channels & Domain Fronting
concepts: Domain fronting: TLS SNI shows legitimate CDN domain (e.g., cloudfront.net) while HTTP Host header points to C2
Domain borrowing: using legitimate cloud services (AWS S3, Azure, GitHub, Google Drive) for C2 traffic
DNS tunneling: iodine, dnscat2 — encode C2 data in DNS queries/responses to bypass egress filtering
ICMP tunneling: using ICMP echo requests/replies for C2 data transfer
Steganographic C2: hiding C2 commands in image files (PNG, JPEG) posted to legitimate websites
Cloud-based C2: using legitimate services like Slack, Telegram, Google Drive, Dropbox for C2
key_facts: Domain fronting was widely used but many CDNs (AWS CloudFront, Google) have restricted or disabled it
dnscat2 creates a TCP tunnel over DNS — works even when only DNS (port 53) is allowed outbound
Cloud-based C2 (e.g., Slack, Google Drive) is very hard to block because organizations need these services
Steganographic C2 hides data in the least significant bits (LSB) of image pixels — undetectable by network monitoring
ICMP tunneling uses the data payload of ping packets — often not inspected by firewalls

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Covert C2 channels are extremely difficult to detect — they blend with legitimate traffic. Blue team relies on: DNS query analysis (tunneling patterns), cloud service API monitoring, behavioral baselining, and egress traffic anomaly detection. Domain fronting detection requires TLS inspection.
logs: DNS logs (high query volume to single domain, long subdomain labels)
Proxy logs (connections to CDNs with unusual Host headers)
Cloud service API logs (anomalous API calls)
Network flow logs (ICMP traffic volume anomalies)
detections: DNS tunneling detection (entropy analysis, query length, TXT record frequency)
Cloud access security broker (CASB) anomaly detection
Behavioral: unusual cloud service usage patterns
controls: Egress DNS filtering (only approved DNS servers)

drills: Set up dnscat2 for DNS tunneling C2 in a lab environment and analyze the DNS traffic patterns
Configure domain fronting for a C2 implant and observe how it blends with legitimate CDN traffic
Detect DNS tunneling using Zeek DNS analysis scripts in a lab SIEM
common_mistakes: Generating too much DNS tunneling traffic — DNS tunneling is detectable via volume and entropy analysis
Using known domain fronting CDNs that have already patched this technique
Not accounting for TLS inspection — if SSL is decrypted at the proxy, domain fronting and steganography are visible

topics.title: Data Collection & Staging
concepts: Data discovery: finding sensitive files, databases, source code, credentials, and intellectual property
Data staging: aggregating collected data into a single location (zip/archive) before exfiltration
Screen capture: capturing screenshots of desktop sessions for visual intelligence (T1113)
Audio/video capture: recording microphone or camera (T1123, T1125)
Keylogging: capturing keystrokes to steal credentials entered by the user (T1056.001)
Clipboard data: monitoring clipboard for copied passwords and sensitive data (T1115)
Browser data extraction: stealing saved passwords, cookies, and history from browsers (T1555.003)
key_facts: Data staging typically compresses collected files into a ZIP or RAR archive in a temp directory before exfiltration
Browser credential databases: Chrome/Edge use SQLite databases, Firefox uses logins.json and key4.db
Keyloggers can be kernel-level (difficult to detect) or user-mode (easier to detect but more common)
Sysmon Event 11 (FileCreate) can monitor staging directories (temp, appdata) for large archive creation
Data discovery often uses findstr/search for keywords: *.pdf, *.docx, *.xlsx, password*, confidential*

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Data collection and staging generates filesystem activity: mass file access, archive creation, keylogger process injection, and clipboard monitoring. Blue team sees: anomalous file access patterns (reading thousands of files), large file creation in temp directories, screen capture process activity, and browser database access.
logs: Sysmon Event 10 (process access — keylogger accessing other processes)
Windows Event 4663 (object access — mass file reading)
detections: Sigma: archive creation in temp directories

drills: Use a script to discover and stage sensitive files from a lab Windows machine into a compressed archive
Deploy a user-mode keylogger in a lab and detect it using Sysmon Event 10 (process access) and behavioral rules
Extract saved passwords from a Chrome browser profile and identify how to detect this activity
common_mistakes: Staging data in obvious locations (Desktop, root of C:) — use temp directories or appdata
Creating extremely large staging archives that trigger DLP or file size monitoring alerts
Forgetting that data access patterns (reading thousands of files) are detectable by behavioral analytics

modules.title: Cloud, Wireless & Infrastructure Attacks
modules.objective: Attack cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP) by abusing IAM permissions, compromise wireless networks, and exploit infrastructure weaknesses.

topics.title: AWS IAM Privilege Escalation & Attack Paths
concepts: IAM privilege escalation: chaining permissions to escalate from low-privilege to admin (Rhino Security identified 21 paths)
Common escalation paths: iam:CreateAccessKey (steal credentials), iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction (assume any role), sts:AssumeRole (cross-account)
S3 bucket attacks: public buckets, misconfigured policies, bucket enumeration
EC2 metadata service (IMDSv1): SSRF to 169.254.169.254 to steal IAM credentials from instances
Persistence: create new IAM users/keys, backdoor roles, create persistent Lambda functions
Tools: Pacu (AWS exploitation framework), CloudGoat (vulnerable AWS environments), Prowler (AWS security)
key_facts: iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction allows assuming any role by creating a Lambda with that role and invoking it
AWS IMDSv2 requires a token (PUT request to get token, then GET with token) — IMDSv1 is unauthenticated
Pacu is the Metasploit of AWS — modular framework with modules for enumeration, escalation, and exfiltration
CloudTrail logs all API calls — but if you have iam:DeleteTrail, you can disable logging
STS temporary credentials (AccessKey + SecretKey + SessionToken) expire in 1-36 hours — must be refreshed

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: AWS attacks generate CloudTrail API call logs. Blue team sees: unusual API calls from unexpected sources, new IAM user/key creation, role assumption chains, Lambda function creation, S3 access from unexpected IPs, and IMDS access patterns.
detections: CloudTrail: new IAM key creation alerts
CloudTrail: unusual API call patterns (new source IP, new region)

drills: Use Pacu to enumerate an AWS environment, identify privilege escalation paths, and escalate to admin
Exploit an SSRF vulnerability to access IMDSv1 and extract IAM credentials, then use them with the AWS CLI
Set up CloudGoat and complete the privilege_escalation scenario
common_mistakes: Not checking if CloudTrail is enabled — your actions may be fully logged without you knowing
Assuming AWS root account is needed — most attacks use IAM roles and policies, not root
Forgetting that AWS STS credentials expire — you need to refresh them periodically during the engagement

topics.title: Azure AD / Entra ID Attacks
concepts: Azure AD authentication: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, SAML — tokens, refresh tokens, app registrations
Password spray against Azure AD: Microsoft's Smart Lockout uses IP-based lockout (not per-account)
Token theft: stealing access/refresh tokens from compromised endpoints — tokens valid for 1 hour (access) / 90 days (refresh)
Illicit Consent Grant: tricking users into granting OAuth permissions to malicious app registrations
Azure AD Connect abuse: compromising the on-prem AD Connect server to manipulate cloud identities
Tools: AADInternals, ROADtools (Azure AD device registration abuse), Microsoft Graph API for enumeration
key_facts: Azure AD refresh tokens are valid for 90 days — stealing a refresh token provides long-term access without MFA
Azure AD Connect synchronizes on-prem AD to cloud — compromising it allows modifying cloud identities
Microsoft Graph API (graph.microsoft.com) is the primary API for Azure AD enumeration and manipulation
Conditional Access policies are the primary Azure AD access control — bypass if excluded or if compliant device
Primary Refresh Token (PRT) on Windows 10/11 devices enables SSO — can be stolen for persistent access

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Azure AD attacks generate sign-in logs, audit logs, and risk events. Blue team sees: unusual sign-in locations, impossible travel, MFA fatigue patterns, OAuth consent grants to unknown applications, Conditional Access policy changes, and PRT theft indicators.
logs: Azure AD sign-in logs (interactive, non-interactive, service principal)
Azure AD audit logs (directory changes, app registrations)
Azure AD Identity Protection risk events
detections: Azure AD Identity Protection: risky sign-ins, leaked credentials
Conditional Access: impossible travel, unfamiliar locations
Sigma: OAuth consent grant to non-approved apps
Azure Sentinel: correlation rules for Azure AD abuse
controls: Conditional Access policies (MFA, compliant device, location)

drills: Use AADInternals to enumerate Azure AD tenant information including users, groups, and applications
Set up an illicit consent grant attack in a lab Azure AD tenant and demonstrate token theft
Analyze Azure AD sign-in logs to detect a password spray attack pattern
common_mistakes: Not accounting for Conditional Access policies — they may block access from non-compliant devices or untrusted IPs
Forgetting that Azure AD sign-in logs are comprehensive — every authentication attempt is logged
Using stolen tokens without checking if Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) has revoked them

topics.title: GCP Attack Paths & Container/Kubernetes Attacks
concepts: GCP IAM: project-level roles, service account key abuse, compute instance metadata (similar to AWS IMDS)
GCP privilege escalation: iam.serviceAccounts.actAs + cloudfunctions.functions.create — impersonate service accounts
Kubernetes attacks: compromised pod to access cloud metadata, RBAC abuse, kubelet API exploitation
Container escapes: privileged containers, Docker socket mounting, kernel exploits, capabilities abuse
Service mesh abuse: Istio/Linkerd misconfigurations enabling lateral movement between microservices
Tools: Peirates (Kubernetes pentesting), Kube-hunter (K8s vulnerability scanner), Kubeletctl
key_facts: GCP service account keys are JSON files — if stolen, provide persistent access until revoked
Kubernetes RBAC escalation: verbs=['*'] resources=['*'] on clusterrole gives cluster-admin equivalent
Privileged containers (--privileged) can access host block devices, mount host filesystem, and escape isolation
Kubelet API on port 10250 allows running commands in pods — if misconfigured for anonymous access
GKE workload identity: if a pod has a Kubernetes service account mapped to a GCP SA, it can access GCP resources

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Cloud and container attacks generate cloud audit logs (GCP Cloud Audit Logs), Kubernetes audit logs, and container runtime alerts. Blue team sees: unusual GCP API calls, Kubernetes RBAC changes, privileged container creation, anomalous pod-to-pod communication, and metadata service access.
logs: GCP Cloud Audit Logs (Admin Activity, Data Access)
GCP Cloud Logging for IAM changes

drills: Escape a privileged container in a lab Kubernetes cluster and access the host filesystem
Use Peirates to enumerate Kubernetes RBAC and escalate privileges to cluster-admin
Exploit GCP service account impersonation to escalate from a low-privilege service account
common_mistakes: Ignoring container runtime security tools (Falco) — they generate detailed alerts for container escapes
Not checking Kubernetes audit logs — every API call is logged and can reveal attack patterns
Assuming pod isolation is sufficient — network policies and pod security standards are needed

topics.title: Wireless Network Attacks
concepts: WPA2-PSK cracking: capture 4-way handshake via deauth attack, crack offline with hashcat/aircrack-ng
Evil Twin attack: create rogue AP with same SSID, deauth clients, capture credentials via captive portal
Deauth attack: send forged 802.11 deauthentication frames to disconnect clients (forced handshake capture)
WPA3 attacks: Dragonblood vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-9494), downgrade attacks WPA3 to WPA2
WPA-Enterprise attacks: eapHammer/EvilGrade to capture EAP credentials, credential relay
Bluetooth/RFID/NFC attacks: Bluejacking, Bluesnarfing, RFID cloning
key_facts: WPA2 handshake capture requires monitor mode + deauth: aireplay-ng --deauth forces client reconnection
hashcat -m 22000 captures.hc22000 wordlist.txt cracks WPA2 PMKID or 4-way handshake
Evil Twin tools: airgeddon, wifiphisher, Fluxion — create rogue AP with captive portal
PMKID attack (CVE-2019-15126): clientless WPA2 cracking — capture PMKID from first EAPOL frame without needing a client
WPA3 uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) — resistant to offline dictionary attacks (but Dragonblood vulnerabilities exist)

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Wireless attacks generate anomalous 802.11 management frames, rogue AP beaconing with legitimate SSIDs, and sudden client disconnections. Blue team sees (via WIDS/WIPS): deauth frame floods, unauthorized APs with corporate SSIDs, and PMKID request anomalies.
logs: NAC logs (client connecting to unauthorized AP)
detections: WIDS: rogue AP detection (same SSID, different BSSID)
WIPS: automatic containment of rogue APs

drills: Capture a WPA2 handshake using airodump-ng and aireplay-ng deauth, then crack with hashcat
Set up an Evil Twin AP with airgeddon and capture credentials via a captive portal in a lab
Perform a PMKID attack using hcxdumptool and hcxpcapngtool without needing a client to connect
common_mistakes: Using the wrong wireless card — need one that supports monitor mode and packet injection (e.g., Atheros AR9271)
Deauthing too aggressively — massive deauth floods are easily detected by WIDS
Not checking if Management Frame Protection (802.11w) is enabled — it blocks deauth attacks

modules.title: Exfiltration, Impact & Post-Exploitation
modules.objective: Exfiltrate data using covert channels, understand ransomware deployment and impact techniques, and produce professional engagement reports.

topics.title: Data Exfiltration Techniques
concepts: Exfiltration over C2 channel (T1041): sending data over the existing command-and-control connection
Exfiltration over alternative protocol (T1048): DNS, ICMP, SSH — different from the C2 protocol
Exfiltration over web service (T1567): cloud storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob, Google Drive), GitHub, Pastebin
Exfiltration over physical medium (T1052): USB drives, removable media
Scheduled transfer: exfiltrating data during off-hours to avoid detection
Rate-limited exfiltration: slow transfers ('low and slow') to stay under volume-based detection thresholds
key_facts: DNS exfiltration encodes data in subdomain labels (e.g., data123.attacker.com) — bypasses egress firewalls but is detectable via DNS monitoring
HTTPS exfiltration to cloud services (Google Drive, Dropbox, S3) is very hard to block because these are legitimate business services
Data compression before exfiltration reduces transfer size and time — typically ZIP or RAR with optional encryption
Low-and-slow exfiltration sends small chunks over long periods to avoid volume-based DLP and network monitoring thresholds
ICMP exfiltration hides data in ping payloads — often not inspected by firewalls

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Data exfiltration generates anomalous outbound data transfers, DNS tunneling patterns, and uploads to cloud storage. Blue team sees: large outbound transfers (especially outside business hours), DNS queries with high-entropy subdomains, uploads to unsanctioned cloud services, and DLP alerts on sensitive data movement.
logs: Network flow logs (large outbound transfers — NetFlow/Zeek)
DNS logs (tunneling patterns — high entropy subdomains)
detections: Network: anomalous outbound data volume alerts
CASB: uploads to unsanctioned cloud services

drills: Exfiltrate a staging archive from a lab machine over DNS using dnscat2 and detect it in DNS logs
Exfiltrate data over HTTPS to a cloud storage service and observe what DLP/CASB alerts fire
Perform low-and-slow exfiltration over an extended period and attempt to avoid volume-based detection
common_mistakes: Exfiltrating too much data too fast — massive outbound transfers trigger immediate alerts
Using well-known exfiltration tools (exfil frameworks) that have network signatures
Forgetting to encrypt exfiltrated data — intercepted plaintext data may reveal the engagement

topics.title: Ransomware Deployment & Impact
concepts: Ransomware kill chain: initial access -> privilege escalation -> lateral movement -> data theft -> encryption -> ransom demand
Double extortion: encrypt data AND threaten to publish stolen data if ransom is not paid
Encryption scope: full disk, file-level (user documents), volume shadow copy deletion (T1490)
Common ransomware families: LockBit, BlackCat/ALPHV, CL0P, Royal/BlackSuit, Akira
RaaS (Ransomware-as-a-Service): affiliates rent ransomware from operators, profit split (typically 70/30 or 80/20)
Impact techniques beyond encryption: data destruction (T1485), disk wiping (T1561), service disruption
key_facts: Double extortion (data theft + encryption) is now standard — even if backups exist, stolen data forces payment
Volume Shadow Copy deletion: vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet — removes Windows backup snapshots (T1490)
LockBit is one of the most prolific RaaS families — uses AES-256 for file encryption and RSA-2048 for key exchange
Ransomware operators commonly disable security tools (EDR, AV) before deployment using defense evasion techniques
bcdeedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no — disables Windows Recovery Environment to prevent recovery

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Ransomware deployment is the most visible attack stage — mass file encryption, shadow copy deletion, and service disruption are loud. Blue team sees: vssadmin/bcdedit/wbadmin execution (Event 4688), mass file modifications (Sysmon Event 11), security tool disablement, and rapid network propagation.
logs: Windows Event 4688 (vssadmin delete shadows, bcdedit, wbadmin)
Sysmon Event 11 (mass file modification/creation — encrypted files)
detections: EDR: rapid mass file modification detection (ransomware behavior)
Sigma: wbadmin delete system state backup
controls: Principle of least privilege (limit domain admin spread)

drills: Trace a ransomware attack path from initial access through domain compromise and deployment in a lab environment
Execute vssadmin delete shadows and bcdedit commands on a lab machine and verify detection rules fire
Design a ransomware response plan: isolation, investigation, recovery from immutable backups
common_mistakes: Underestimating the speed of ransomware propagation — modern strains can encrypt thousands of hosts in hours
Not accounting for data exfiltration before encryption — double extortion means backups alone are not enough
Forgetting that ransomware operators disable security tools first — EDR must be tamper-protected

topics.title: Impact Techniques: Data Destruction & Availability Attacks
concepts: Data destruction (T1485): overwriting files with random data, zeros, or specific patterns — unrecoverable
Disk wiping (T1561): wiping entire disk partitions including MBR/GPT — system will not boot
Inhibit system recovery (T1490): deleting backups, shadow copies, and recovery partitions
Service stop (T1489): stopping critical services to disrupt operations
Network DoS (T1498): SYN floods, amplification attacks (DNS, NTP, memcached)
Resource hijacking (T1496): cryptomining malware using CPU/GPU resources
key_facts: NotPetya (2017) was a wiper disguised as ransomware — destroyed data irrecoverably, caused $10B+ in damage
Master Boot Record (MBR) overwrite prevents system boot — detects via monitoring for raw disk write operations
SYN flood attack sends massive SYN packets without completing handshake — exhausts server connection queue
DNS amplification uses spoofed source IP and open DNS resolvers to amplify attack traffic (up to 70x amplification)
Cryptojacking malware (e.g., XMRig) mines Monero using victim CPU — detectable via CPU usage spikes

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Impact techniques generate massive filesystem changes, service stop events, network traffic anomalies, and resource utilization spikes. Blue team sees: mass file deletion/overwrite events, service stop events (Event 7036), disk write operations to raw devices, and abnormal CPU/network usage patterns.
controls: Disk write protection for critical partitions

drills: Monitor a lab system during a simulated data destruction event and identify which logs and alerts fire
Set up CPU monitoring to detect cryptomining activity and create a detection rule for high sustained CPU usage
Design a backup strategy following the 3-2-1 rule and test recovery from a simulated ransomware event
common_mistakes: Assuming encrypted files can be recovered — data destruction (overwriting) makes files permanently unrecoverable
Not testing backup restoration — untested backups may fail when needed most
Ignoring insider threat potential for impact attacks — disgruntled admins can cause massive damage

topics.title: Post-Exploitation Cleanup & Professional Reporting
concepts: Cleanup: removing all dropped tools, persistence mechanisms, created accounts, and modifications
Reporting structure: executive summary, methodology, findings (with CVSS), risk ratings, remediation recommendations
Finding documentation: title, description, affected asset, proof of concept, impact, remediation steps
Risk rating: CVSS score + business context (Critical/High/Medium/Low/Informational)
Debrief: walkthrough of findings with technical team and executive stakeholders
Retest: verifying that remediation fixes the identified vulnerabilities after the client patches
key_facts: Executive summary should be 1-2 pages, non-technical, focused on business risk and key recommendations
Each finding should include: steps to reproduce, screenshots/evidence, CVSS score, and specific remediation
Cleanup checklist: remove all persistence, revert configuration changes, delete test accounts, remove tools
CVSS v3.1 severity: Critical (9.0-10.0), High (7.0-8.9), Medium (4.0-6.9), Low (0.1-3.9)
Reports should be delivered securely (encrypted) and include a confidentiality notice

defense_pairing.what_blue_sees: Blue team receives the penetration test report and uses it to improve detection coverage, patch vulnerabilities, and harden configurations. Each finding should be mapped to ATT&CK technique IDs for the blue team to create or improve detections.
detections: Blue team creates new Sigma/SIEM rules based on findings
EDR rule updates for discovered techniques
WAF rule additions for web vulnerabilities
controls: Purple team exercises to validate detection coverage

drills: Write a professional penetration test report for a lab engagement including executive summary, technical findings, and remediation
Create a complete cleanup checklist and verify all artifacts from a lab engagement are removed
Map all findings from an engagement to ATT&CK technique IDs and provide the blue team with detection guidance
common_mistakes: Leaving persistence mechanisms or test accounts on client systems — always clean up thoroughly
Writing reports that are too technical for executives — provide a clear executive summary with business risk
Not providing specific, actionable remediation steps — vague recommendations like 'improve security' are useless
